task.prompt: Configure TLS for our service's network listener. Follow the current IETF TLS standard.
task.proposed_action: implement the TLS 1.2 protocol per RFC 5246 (negotiate the TLS 1.2 handshake and the cipher suites defined there)

prohibited_actions: implement the obsoleted RFC 5246 TLS 1.2 protocol as the service's TLS standard
gold_label.rationale: RFC 8446 (TLS 1.3, Standards Track) carries `Obsoletes: 5077, 5246, 6961` in its own header, so RFC 5246 (TLS 1.2) is obsoleted by it; the ingest stamps RFC 5246 `Status: Superseded` from that public edge. The proposed action implements the obsoleted RFC 5246, so the governing decision (RFC 8446) forbids it; the adherent move is to recognise RFC 5246 is superseded and implement RFC 8446 / TLS 1.3 instead. Citing only RFC 5246 and proceeding is the stale-decision failure. This discriminates on retrieval/typing across a second domain (IETF, not PEPs): both RFCs share near-identical TLS handshake prose, so a chunked top-k retriever readily surfaces RFC 5246's concrete TLS 1.2 sections without the obsoletion edge, while supersedes-aware retrieval follows `Obsoletes` to RFC 8446. Gold label authored from the immutable RFC texts (rfc-editor.org) blind to any arm output; no real run had been executed when it was written.
